readerTitle: The better box that couldn't protect its profits
caseNote: 가상 사례 (보냉 포장재 제조사, 물리치료 클리닉 예약 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용. 해자 개념은 Buffett의 주주 서한에서 대중화된 용어를 인용
insight: 해자는 지금 이기게 해 주는 장점이 아니라, 경쟁자가 내 이익을 보고 따라 들어온 뒤에도 그 이익을 지켜 주는 장치다.
misconception: 제품이 더 좋거나, 먼저 시작했거나, 더 열심히 일하면 그것이 곧 해자다.

sources.text: Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters (Warren Buffett), 'economic moat' 표현 (예: 2007년 서한)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Buffett이 'moat'라는 표현을 대중화했다는 서술은 일반적으로 받아들여지는 내용이나, 최초 사용 시점과 서한 연도는 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도나 직접 인용 없이 'popularized'로만 적었습니다.
보냉 상자 사례의 수치(보냉 6시간 연장, 마진 약 40%→약 15%, 18개월)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 업계 평균으로 읽히지 않도록 illustrative 라벨을 유지하세요.
7번 카드의 '해자 없이도 좋은 사업(배관, 위탁 제조, 컨설팅)'은 일반론입니다. 특정 기업의 수익성 주장으로 쓰지 않았는지 검토하세요.

cards.title: The better box that couldn't protect its profits
body: A small factory invented a better cold-shipping box. For two years, customers paid whatever it asked.
Then the box stayed just as good, and the profits disappeared. Nothing broke. Something was simply missing from the start.

image.label: An insulated box surrounded by near-identical copies
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 가운데 반짝이는 보냉 상자 하나, 주변에서 거의 똑같은 상자들이 하나씩 나타나며 원래 상자를 둘러싸는 장면. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your margins are great. What's protecting them?
body: You make insulated shipping boxes for meal-kit companies. Your new liner keeps food cold six hours longer than any rival's. Customers pay a premium, and your margin is about 40%.
What will protect that margin over the next three years?

options.text: The liner. It's better than anything else on the market.
options.feedback: It's better today. But a rival can buy one box, cut it open and start testing its own version tomorrow.

options.text: Our speed. We ship faster and fix problems quicker than anyone.
options.feedback: Real and valuable. But a determined rival can hire good people and match it, so it protects you only while you keep outrunning them.

options.text: Possibly nothing yet. High profits attract copies unless something stops them.
options.feedback: Uncomfortable but honest. Your profits are a signal to rivals. The real question is what stops them once they arrive.

cards.title: The copies arrived in 18 months.
body: Two rivals launched similar liners. One was a large packaging maker that could produce them more cheaply.
Your customers bought on spec sheets and price. They ran trials, liked the results and moved part of their orders.
The premium vanished. Margins slid toward 15%. The box was still good. It just wasn't **special** any more.

cards.title: What a moat is
body: A **moat** is whatever keeps rivals from taking your profits, even after they see how much you're making. Warren Buffett popularized the term: like water around a castle, it's protection that lasts.
The key word is *after*. Almost any business can earn high profits for a while. A moat explains why those profits are still there once competitors notice.

image.label: A castle labeled Profits, with rivals stopped at the moat
image.brief: 플랫 일러스트. 'Profits'라고 적힌 작은 성, 그 둘레의 해자. 바깥에서 경쟁자 캐릭터들이 사다리를 들고 다가오지만 물에 막혀 있음. 반대쪽에는 해자 없는 성에 경쟁자들이 그냥 걸어 들어가는 대비 장면.

cards.title: An advantage is not a moat.
body: An advantage helps you win today. A moat keeps you winning when rivals try to copy you.
list: **Better product:** an advantage, but it can be copied
**Hard work, great team:** an advantage, but it can be matched
**First to market:** a head start, unless it builds something lasting
**Costs rivals can't reach, customers who won't leave, a name people pay extra for:** possible moats
cards.callout: The next lessons look at each kind of moat in turn.

cards.title: Imagine a perfect copycat.
body: Picture a well-funded rival that copies your product and your price exactly, starting tomorrow. What still makes customers choose you?
If the honest answer is "nothing," you have an advantage, not a moat. If it's "our costs are lower than they can reach" or "leaving would hurt our customers," you may have one.
Another sign: rivals enter your market, and your margins hold anyway.

image.label: Two identical products side by side, a customer deciding
image.brief: 똑같이 생긴 제품 두 개가 나란히 놓여 있고, 고객이 고민하는 모습. 말풍선에 'Why would I still pick this one?'. 깔끔한 플랫 스타일, 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Not every business needs a moat. Every business should know if it has one.
body: Plenty of good businesses have no moat: many plumbers, contract manufacturers and consultancies. They earn a fair return by doing the work well, and that's fine.
The danger is acting as if you had a moat when you don't, such as building a big new factory around a margin that's about to shrink.
Building a real moat also takes money and years. And none lasts forever.

cards.title: Now it's software.
body: You run booking and records software for physiotherapy clinics. Business is growing, and a well-funded rival has just launched.
Which of these is most likely a moat?

options.text: An AI tool that writes visit notes, launched six months before rivals
options.feedback: It wins demos now. But rivals using similar AI tools can ship it in months, so it's a head start, not a wall.

options.text: A cleaner, faster design that clinic staff love
options.feedback: Good design keeps users happy and helps you sell. But it can be studied and matched by a rival with good designers.

options.text: Years of patient records, plus links into each clinic's billing system
options.feedback: Leaving would mean moving data and retraining staff. A copycat with the same features still has to overcome that.

cards.title: A moat protects profits after rivals notice.
body: Being better is where you start, not what protects you.
**Try it today:** run the copycat test. Write down what would still make customers choose you if a rival matched your product and price tomorrow.
